title: Two swords
hookLine: the young sixth Guru wears two swords, one for worldly duty and one for the spirit

cards: Picture the boy. His name is Hargobind, he's about eleven, and his father has just been killed in Lahore. Now he is the sixth Guru, and the whole community is watching him, grieving and frightened.
What will he be? Up to now the Gurus have carried no weapons. They've been teachers, poets, builders of pools and kitchens.
On the day he is formally installed as Guru, old Baba Buddha, the man who read the first hukam, brings out the things a Guru is given. And the boy asks for something new. A sword.

teach.b: Two words, two swords. Miri comes from mir, the Persian word for a ruler or commander: worldly authority, the business of protecting people and running things.
Piri comes from pir, a spiritual guide: spiritual authority, the inner life, the Name.
Guru Hargobind wore one sword for each, on either side. His meaning was plain. After what happened in Lahore, faith would not be defenseless.
The Guru would still be a guide of souls, and also a leader who could protect his people.
He began to keep horses and train fighters, and Sikhs were asked to bring weapons and horses as offerings along with everything else. Here's what's easy to miss.

The two swords were not two separate lives, a religious one on Sunday and a practical one the rest of the week. Sikhs understand the point as the opposite: the worldly sword must be guided by the spiritual one.
Power without the Name becomes cruelty; the Name without care for the world can walk away from people who are suffering.
Many Sikhs describe the ideal as saint and soldier in one person.
You can still see the two swords today. The Khanda, the emblem on Sikh flags, has a double-edged blade in the center, and on either side curves a sword, often explained as miri and piri. Two swords.

how: Sikhs honor Guru Hargobind's two swords of miri and piri as the ideal of the saint-soldier, and the two curved swords of the Khanda emblem on the Sikh flag are often explained as miri and piri.

o: the two kinds of war: attack and defense
a duel between two rival swordsmen
worldly and spiritual power held together

games.q: what's inside the two swords — tap the pairs.

s: the earlier Gurus also carried swords
up to Guru Hargobind, the Gurus carried no weapons. the two swords were something new.
the two swords mean two separate lives
Sikhs understand them as one: the spiritual guides the worldly.
the Khanda emblem is often linked to miri and piri
its two curved swords on either side are often explained that way.

games.q: you're eleven, your father has just been killed, and today you're installed as Guru. Baba Buddha brings the traditional gifts. what do you ask for?
o: nothing new: keep things as they were.
two swords, one for the world and one for the spirit.
a bodyguard, so you can stay hidden.
games.why: Guru Hargobind asked for two swords, miri and piri. faith would stay a guide of souls, and it would also protect its people.

practice: If you can, stand tall for thirty seconds: feet under your hips, spine long, shoulders down, chin level.

Feel both hands at your sides, one holding what you have to take care of, work, bills, people who depend on you, the other holding the quiet center you come back to. Then sit, and keep that same tallness, both sides held together.

wordCard.voice: Miri piri. Worldly authority and spiritual authority, worn by Guru Hargobind as two swords, the spirit guiding the world.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi, from Persian mir (ruler) and pir (spiritual guide).

carryVoice: Your line: two swords, one heart. Tomorrow, the young Guru builds a seat. Day sixty-five.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition on Guru Hargobind's installation and the two swords of miri and piri, 1606
